name: Colin Patel

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time for this. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government, and we don't sell anything. Everything you tell me stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I share-farm 220 hectares with an older couple, the Ashdowns, who own the land and want to stay on it without doing the work. I bring the labour and most of the machinery, they bring the land, and we split what it makes. It's wheat, oilseed rape and about 150 store cattle I buy in as youngsters and finish over the winter. In summer I also go out baling for six neighbours, which pays for the baler and a bit more. My partner Priya does the books at the vet practice in town, and the kids, Ravi and Asha, are thirteen and nine.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Weather, mostly. You can plan all you like and then it rains for nine days in August. I'll use an AI chat thing now and then to check spray rules or ask about a weather window, but I double-check everything it says. I've been caught out by a confident answer before.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine by me. I'd half expected that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's useful but overhyped, which is what I'd say about most things in the farming papers. I'd be fair about it, though. It does save a bit of time on the paperwork.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means the arrangement with the Ashdowns carries on, and the baling keeps paying. That's good. My worries would be the same as now: grain prices, fertiliser costs and whether Mr Ashdown's kids sell the land when he goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going exactly as I am. I'd use the chat tool a bit more for the spray records, maybe. And we'd keep up the 180 a month savings and think about a newer baler in a couple of years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Nothing much changes, which is what I'd want.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me about the Ashdowns' kids.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There are two, both in the city, both lovely, neither has any interest in farming. When the old man who owns the land I farm goes, his kids will want their share out. That's the real threat to me, more than any robot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you spend that time saved on paperwork on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably more paperwork, if I'm honest. There's always a new form. But maybe I'd get to one more of Ravi's football matches.

S0.say: It's useful but overhyped, like most things in the farming papers. To be fair, it does save a bit of time on paperwork.
S0.think: The arrangement with the Ashdowns carries on and the baling keeps paying. My real worries stay grain prices, fertiliser costs and whether the Ashdowns' children sell the land.
S0.do: Keeps going exactly as he is and uses the chat tool more for spray records. Keeps saving 180 a month and thinks about a newer baler in a couple of years.
S0.quote: When the old man who owns the land I farm goes, his kids will want their share out. That's the real threat to me, more than any robot.
S0.fieldNote: Colin is careful and even-handed, praising and doubting AI in the same breath. His biggest worry sits outside technology: the landowners' heirs selling the land. He uses AI only with double-checking.

steps.text: Keep share-farming the Ashdowns' 220 hectares and baling for six neighbours
Keep saving 180 a month towards a newer baler in a couple of years

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's probably the realistic one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say farmers have always adapted and we'll adapt again. I'd also say you don't buy the first version of anything. Let someone else iron out the problems.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the baling goes first. Two of my six neighbours are already talking about a shared self-driving baler. That's maybe a third of my summer income gone, and I'd still be paying off my own baler.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd watch who buys what and talk to the neighbours about a fair deal, maybe I run their shared machine for them. I'd save harder, 250 a month, in case the baling money drops. And I'd start using the AI tools properly for the cattle records, because that's the way it's going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's the baling money I'd fret about, not the farm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to the neighbours who buy the self-driving baler?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good luck with the self-driving baler, and call me when it breaks down in a wet field. I'd mean it kindly, mostly. I'd be glad to be the man who knows how to get it going again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there any part of the farm itself you'd want to automate?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe the cattle feeding, once I've seen it work on three or four farms. Not before. I've seen a feed robot go wrong at a show and it was not pretty.

S1.say: Farmers have always adapted and we'll adapt again. But you don't buy the first version of anything; let someone else iron out the problems.
S1.think: The baling goes first. Two of my six neighbours are already talking about a shared self-driving baler, which is maybe a third of my summer income.
S1.do: Watches what neighbours buy and offers to run their shared baler for them. Saves harder at 250 a month and starts using AI tools properly for cattle records.
S1.feel: Uneasy about the baling income rather than the farm.
S1.quote: Good luck with the self-driving baler, and call me when it breaks down in a wet field.
S1.fieldNote: Colin pinpoints the most exposed part of his income: summer contract baling. His approach is to wait for proof and position himself as the person who can fix the machines. He'd automate only after seeing it work on several farms.

steps.text: Watch who buys the shared self-driving baler and offer to run it for them
Save 250 a month in case the summer baling money drops
Start using AI tools properly for the 150 store cattle's records

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Thinking work in 2028. That's Priya's job, not mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say farmers have got a few more years than the office people this time, and we should use them sensibly instead of panicking. At the machinery ring I'd tell the neighbours not to buy the first robot that turns up in 2031. I'd say it fairly calmly, because that's how I say most things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, the first hit is at home, not on the farm. Priya does the books at the vet practice, and books are exactly what the AI does in 2028. My own work is hands-on, so the cattle and the baling should hold till about 2031, but then the Ashdowns could farm the land with a robot and a computer and not need me at all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the baler for two more summers and sell it in 2030, before every second-hand baler in the country hits the market at once. That's maybe 18,000 if I time it right. Priya would start looking for work at the practice that's with the animals, not the computer, maybe as a vet nurse, which needs a two-year course. We'd lift our savings to 250 a month while I've still got the baling money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but steady. It's like seeing rain coming on the forecast when the hay's still down: you know what you've got to do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Priya say about retraining?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd grumble and then do it better than anyone. She's already the one who holds the calves for the vet when they're short-handed. Priya would be fine with blood and muck; it's the course fees that would worry her, about 3,000 a year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Have you thought about talking to the Ashdowns?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want to, early, before their kids start reading about robot farms. I'd ask Mr Ashdown for a five-year agreement in writing. A handshake was enough for twelve years, but a handshake won't stand up against a robot that works for free.

S2.say: Farmers have a few more years than the office people this time, and we should use them sensibly instead of panicking. Nobody should buy the first robot that turns up in 2031.
S2.think: The first hit is at home: Priya does the books at the vet practice, and that's exactly what the AI does in 2028. My cattle and baling should hold until about 2031, but then the Ashdowns could farm with a robot and not need me.
S2.do: Keeps the baler two more summers and sells it in 2030 for about 18,000, before the second-hand market floods. Backs Priya's move to a two-year vet nurse course, raises savings to 250 a month and asks the Ashdowns for a five-year written agreement.
S2.feel: Anxious but steady, like seeing rain on the forecast with the hay still down.
S2.quote: A handshake was enough for twelve years, but a handshake won't stand up against a robot that works for free.
S2.fieldNote: Colin saw at once that the thinking AI hits his partner's bookkeeping before it touches his own hands-on work. His answer is all about timing: sell the baler before prices fall, and get the share-farming deal in writing early. He worries, but in a planner's way, and the three years of farm income are what keep him from real alarm.

steps.text: Sell the baler in 2030 for about 18,000, before second-hand prices fall
Raise savings to 250 a month while the baling money still comes in
Help Priya pay for a two-year vet nurse course, about 3,000 a year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years, then three more. Good. Time to watch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the sensible pace, and I'd tell the neighbours we've got time to do it properly. Let the big farms try the robots first. I'd still say you don't buy version one of anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think it's manageable. Priya's work changes in 2031, so she'd have five years to move into the vet nursing side, and my farm work holds till 2034. The baling goes when the self-driving balers come, and I'd be 51 with the cattle and the Ashdowns' land, if their kids haven't sold it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the baler for four summers and sell it in 2033. Around year two, once robots have proven themselves on a few farms locally, I'd do a farm robot operation and repair course at the college. And I'd push savings up to 300 a month in the last two years before the robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in control. I'd have a plan written on the back of a feed invoice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why sell the baler in 2033 and not now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because it's still earning. Selling the baler in a panic now would cost me maybe 12,000. Timing's half of farming, and the other half is the weather.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Ravi be doing by then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ravi would be eighteen in 2031. He likes tinkering with the quad bike, so maybe an engineering apprenticeship. I'd want him working on the robots, not competing with them.

S3.say: This is the sensible pace, and we've got time to do it properly. Let the big farms try the robots first, because you don't buy version one of anything.
S3.think: It's manageable: Priya has five years to move into vet nursing before 2031, and my farm work holds until 2034. I'd be 51 with the cattle and the Ashdowns' land, if their kids haven't sold it.
S3.do: Keeps the baler for four summers and sells it in 2033. Takes a farm robot operation and repair course around year two, once robots have proven themselves locally, and raises savings to 300 a month in the last two years.
S3.feel: Uneasy but in control, with a plan written on the back of a feed invoice.
S3.quote: Selling the baler in a panic now would cost me maybe 12,000. Timing's half of farming, and the other half is the weather.
S3.fieldNote: Colin treats this timeline as a timing problem he knows how to solve. He'd retrain only once he's seen robots work locally, which fits his habit of waiting for proof. He wants his son to work on the machines rather than against them.

steps.text: Keep the baler four more summers and sell it in 2033
Take a farm robot operation and repair course at the college in year two
Raise savings to 300 a month in the two years before the robots

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Thirteen years until a robot can bale. That's a long run.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, as long as people don't waste it. In the farming group chat I'd say watch, learn, then buy together. Nothing clever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be fine. I'd be 56 by 2039, Priya would have years to change her work, and the kids would be grown. The bigger question is the land, because Mr Ashdown is 74 now and that's a lot more certain than any robot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd watch for the first couple of years and change nothing. Around year three I'd buy a share in a robot cattle feeder with two neighbours, maybe 8,000 each. And I'd start putting 60 a month into a fund for Ravi and Asha's training.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A long run-up suits someone like me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why buy a robot feeder at all, if your own work is safe for years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I want to learn it while it's my choice. I'd rather be the third person who buys a farm robot than the first, but I don't want to be the last either. The last one pays full price and learns in a rush.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the land matters more. What would you do about that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Talk to the Ashdowns' kids about a long lease or buying a slice of the land, once they inherit. I'd want that settled before 2039. A robot can't farm land it isn't allowed on.

S4.say: Ten years is plenty, as long as people don’t waste it. My advice to the neighbours is watch, learn, then buy the machines together.
S4.think: I'd be fine, aged 56 by 2039 with grown kids and Priya having years to change her work. The bigger question is the land, because Mr Ashdown is 74 now and that's more certain than any robot.
S4.do: Watches for the first couple of years and changes nothing, then buys a share in a robot cattle feeder with two neighbours around year three for about 8,000. Starts a 60-a-month fund for Ravi and Asha's training.
S4.feel: Calm, mostly. A long run-up suits him.
S4.quote: I'd rather be the third person who buys a farm robot than the first, but I don't want to be the last either.
S4.fieldNote: With thirteen years before robots, Colin is relaxed and keeps returning to the land question rather than technology. He wants to learn robots while it's still his choice, not in a rush. His plan is cautious and well-paced, very much in character.

steps.text: Change nothing on the farm for the first couple of years
Buy a share in a robot cattle feeder with two neighbours for about 8,000
Put 60 a month into a fund for Ravi and Asha's training

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because Priya's job doing the books would go first, and then my baling and the share-farming deal three years after, before anything was proven. What would help is plain information about which machines actually work, and help to buy them jointly with neighbours instead of each farm going alone.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You could have asked about the land itself. Whoever owns the land does fine, whatever AI does. People like me who just work the land are the ones in the middle.

headlineQuote: Whoever owns the land does fine, whatever AI does. People like me who just work the land are the ones in the middle.
portrait: Colin Patel, 43, share-farms 220 hectares of wheat, oilseed rape and store cattle with an older landowning couple, and earns extra from summer contract baling. He uses AI now and then but double-checks it, and waits for proof before buying anything. He's calm if AI stalls and uneasy about losing baling income under steady change. Fast AGI makes him anxious because his partner's bookkeeping job goes in 2028 and his own farm work three years later, so he'd time the sale of his baler and help her retrain as a vet nurse. With five or ten years he relaxes, retrains or buys shared machines once they're proven, and sees the landowners' ageing as the bigger risk.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because his partner's bookkeeping job would go first and his baling and share-farming deal three years later, before any machine was proven.
whatWouldHelp: Plain information on which machines actually work, and help to buy them jointly with neighbouring farms.
